title: Add way to swallow spurious warnings
body:
Two files are provided:
- detail/disable_warnings.hpp,
  which stores the user warnings, and disable some of them, and
- detail/re_enable_warnings.hpp,
  which restores the user warnings.

These files are ment to be included multiple times.

They disable spurious warnings for a code block between
disable_warnings.hpp and re_enable_warnings.hpp

Currently GCC and clang are supported, and Wshadow is the only warning
swallowed in the algorithm.hpp and view.hpp headers.

Support for other compilers/warnings can easily be added.

Rationale: it is better to swallow spurious warnings produced by broken
compilers or insane warning configurations than to waste time modifying
valid and correct code.

title: travis-ci integration
body:
**Travis-CI** support (results for the branch are [here](https://travis-ci.org/gnzlbg/range-v3/builds/29970297)).

Travis-ci is a continuous integration framework that;
- builds the test in debug, release, and with asan using both gcc and clang,
- runs the tests for all commits, pull-requests, etc and shows the results next to them on github. 

Its main limitation is that it is Linux only, and right now it supports gcc 4.8, and clang 3.4.
More tools can be integrated (easily: valgrind, clang-format, clang static-analyzer, UBSan, harder: MSan). 

**Note to Eric**: you need to activate travis-ci by logging into its website with your github account. IIRC you might also need to choose there which of your repos it should scan (it might do it automatically).

**Updated CMake File**: 
- added Release and Debug builds (we can discuss the flags here), and 
- factored out the path of libcxx (more about this below).

Since libcxx is only officially supported on Mac, CMake has no "find_libcxx" script, and even using it on Mac can be a pain, the easiest is to manually provide the `include` and `lib` (this works for linux, mac, and windows, as well as for those with multiple libcxx versions). I recommend using a script to avoid writing:

``` bash
cmake . -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE="Release/Debug" \
-DLIBCXX_INCLUDE_DIR="path-to-libcxx/include" \
-DLIBCXX_LIB_DIR="path-to-libcxx/lib" 
```

This one works on Mac and Linux: 

``` bash
#!/bin/bash
export LIBCXX_DIRS="-DLIBCXX_INCLUDE_DIR=\"path-to-libcxx/include\" -DLIBCXX_LIB_DIR=\"path-to-libcxx/lib\" "

while getopts "drhx" option
do
    case "${option}" in
        h)
            echo "Following build modes are available:"
            echo "-d    Debug"
            echo "-r    Release"
            exit 1
            ;;
        d)
            eval "cmake $LIBCXX_DIRS -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug"
            echo "Debug configuration finished!"
            exit 1
            ;;
        r)
            eval "cmake $LIBCXX_DIRS -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release"
            echo "Release configuration finished!"
            exit 1
            ;;
    esac
done
```

title: Return SizedIteratorRanges from ranges::range for RandomAccessIteratorRanges and SizedIterables
body:
The interface of `ranges::range` consists of:
- `ranges::range(Iterator, Sentinel, Size) -> sized_iterator_range`
- `ranges::range(Iterator, Sentinel) -> iterator_range`

However, when calling `ranges::range(Iterator, Sentinel)` with `RandomAccessIterator`s, we can 
compute the range size in `O(1)` and return a `sized_iterator_range`.

Furthermore, some containers like `std::list` provide only `BidirectionalIterator`s, but they have
an `O(1)` `size()` member function.

This patch changes `ranges::range` interface to: 
- `ranges::range(Iterator, Sentinel, Size) -> sized_iterator_range`
- `ranges::range(Iterator, Sentinel) -> sized_iterator_range` (if possible) / `iterator_range`
- `ranges::range(Iterable&) -> sized_iterator_range` (if possible) / `iterator_range`

The `ranges::range(Iterable&)` dispatches to a `sized_iterator_range` if the `Iterable` has `RandomAccessIterator`s or `ranges::size(Iterable&)` can compute its size (which is `O(1)`). Otherwise it returns an `iterator_range`.

Note:  the `algorithm/equal.cpp` test used to perform one comparison in the modified `CHECK` clause when comparing two `RandomAccessRange`s even tho they had different sizes. Now it doesn't need to perform any comparison at all.

title: Implement zip with interms of zip
body:
Implementation of zip algorithm as the primitive operation for typelist leads to code that I consider as easier to understand.

The original implementation of zip_with creates a typefunction by chaining bind multiple times for each corresponding set of typelist elements. I mean that invocation of zip_with on list (a1, b1, c1) and (a2, b2, c2) will create following list with following functors:
  (bind(bind(f, a1, _all), _a2, _all), bind(bind(f, b1, _all), _b2, _all))
Which invocation will result of creating list that contains
  (f(a1, a2), f(b1, b2)).

The implementation of zip provided in this commit implements the zip function as the adding corresponding typelist elements to corresponding typelist of initial list of empty list. I consider this implementation as more intuitive.

title: Removes view::filter from view.hpp
body:
This removes `filter.hpp` from `view.hpp`, which will allow to: 

``` c++
#include <range/v3/all.hpp> 
#define RANGES_NO_DEPRECATED_WARNING
#include <range/v3/view/filter.hpp>
#undef RANGES_NO_DEPRECATED_WARNING
```

I think it is good practice to don't pull in any deprecated functionality by default. The whole point of the deprecated warning is to warn the user that some functionality they are using can be removed in the future. Once the user knows, it should be allowed to disable this warning selectively. 

However, the deprecation attribute does not let the user disable the usage of a specific warning at the declaration level. The user can disable the warnings at the call level, but if you want to disable a specific warning (e.g. the usage of filter) for a single TU, there is no way to specify that you want to disable that warning _only_: `-Wno-deprecated` disables all deprecation warnings. 

One can _try_ to selectively disable a single deprecation warning by modifying the warning level at every point of usage. This however, requires something like: 

``` c++
auto rng = stuff | stuff |
            // modify warning level
            filter
            // modify warning level
            | stuff | stuff;
```

which is far from ideal.

title: Lazy distance comparison for NonSizedIterable
body:
I often need to compare the size of a (possibly large) bidirectional range `rng` with a small number `n`. When the range is large, computing the "full" length (i.e. `distance(rng)`) is inefficient for this purpose; it's enough to compute "partial" length at most `n` or `n + 1`. I came up with the following solutions to this problem: ### A. "drop at most" range adaptor Oven's [`dropped(n)`](http://p-stade.sourceforge.net/oven/doc/html/oven/range_adaptors.html#oven.range_adaptors.dropped) range adaptor drops at most `n` elements; it does not penetrate the end of the range even if the range has size less than `n`. (To differentiate it from range-v3's `drop` adaptor, I call it `drop_at_most`.) With this adaptor, we can make comparison without computing the "full" length. For example, `distance(rng) < n` <--> `empty(rng | drop_at_most(n - 1))` `distance(rng) > n` <--> `!empty(rng | drop_at_most(n))` ### B. "bounded distance" function `bounded_distance(rng, bound)` returns the size of `rng` if the size is less than `bound`, and returns `bound` otherwise. This function increments an iterator at most `bound` times. For example, `distance(rng) < n` <--> `bounded_distance(rng, n) < n` `distance(rng) > n` <--> `bounded_distance(rng, n + 1) > n` ### C. "lazy distance" proxy `lazy_distance(rng)` returns a proxy that can be compared with a number. Actual computation of "partial" length is done when a proxy is compared. For example, `distance(rng) < n` <--> `lazy_distance(rng) < n` `distance(rng) > n` <--> `lazy_distance(rng) > n`
However, IMHO, Option A is not so intuitive and Option B is verbose (we need to write `n` twice). I like Option C _very much_, but this approach might be too complex for a simple task and it might be difficult to get into the Standard. Then I sought another solution and found that the [GHC API](https://downloads.haskell.org/~ghc/latest/docs/html/libraries/ghc/Util.html) has interesting function: ``` listLengthCmp :: [a] -> Int -> Ordering ``` I use this function interface as a fourth solution. ### D. "lazy distance comparison" function `distance_compare(rng, n)` returns positive (negative) integers if the size of `rng` is larger (smaller) than `n` and returns 0 if the size equals `n`. For example, `distance(rng) < n` <--> `distance_compare(rng, n) < 0` `distance(rng) > n` <--> `distance_compare(rng, n) > 0`
Option D is less readable than Option C, but it has good balance between the conciseness of the approach and the readability. This PR implemented `distance_compare` (Option D) and tests. What do you think?

title: Constexpr support
body:
Adds C++14 constexpr support
- adds macros to detect the language version: 
  - `RANGES_CXX_GREATER_THAN_11` for C++>11 (e.g. C++14/17/...)
  - `RANGES_CXX_GREATER_THAN_14` for C++>14 (e.g. C++17/...)
- adds macro to enable relaxed constexpr support in C++>11:
  - `RANGES_RELAXED_CONSTEXPR` 
  - note in C++11 the macro is defined to `inline`
- add CMake option to choose with which language std the tests should be compiled:
  - `-DRANGES_CXX_STD=value` => `-std=c++value`,  `value={11,14,17,1y,1z}` (defaults to `11`).
- set up travis to test in both C++11 and C++14
- set up travis to test with:
  - gcc-4.9 (libstdc++)
  - clang-3.4, clang-3.5, clang-3.6, clang-3.7 (libc++)
- set up valgrind with CMake and travis 
  - note: all tests are run both with and without valgrind in all configurations
- add utilities: 
  - constexpr friendly array (used for testing)
  - constexpr reverse_iterator (used for rbegin/rend/...)

**Lessons learned**
- [x] `constexpr` functions are instantiated in unevaluated contexts (yes, really!)
  - Solution: don't use `-> decltype(...)` for SFINAE. Seriously, just don't, use `enable_if` or similar instead. 
  - Otherwise... different branches will be taken at compile time in C++14 is some of the functions involved are marked `constexpr`. This is particularly bad for customization points since some users might mark theirs `constexpr` and others won't. The alternatives are more verbose but work fine and are in general more explicit (concepts, enable_if, ...). 
  - In a nutshell: your code shall not break when removing the trailing return types (`-> decltype(...)`) in C++14.

**Currently work-in-progress ("// TODO: [constexpr]")**:
- [ ] Set up travis to test range-v3 under MacOS using AppleClang + libc++.
- [ ] -Wundefined-inline: `constexpr` implies `inline` which introduces some visibility warnings.
- [x] Rethink general workarounds:
  - [x] `std::bind` is not `constexpr` (a one parameter parameter "binder" `binder_` is implemented in functional)
  - [x] `constexpr` functions are instantiated in unevaluated contexts (out of luck here)
- [x] Open issues (haven't given them enough thought):
  - [x] Should only non-mutable algorithms/views be implemented? 
    - No, mutable algorithms/views can also be made constexpr and used in a "non-constexpr"y way inside `constexpr` functions.
    - Old note: mutating `begin` and `end` member functions cannot mutate the algorithm state if this is `constexpr`. Update: but this is not `constexpr` if not marked as such inside a `constexpr` function. 
  - [x] Should actions be implemented?
    - Yes, same rationale as for mutable algorithms/views.
- [ ] Clean-up: fix all todos, rebase, remove all whitespace changes, ...
  - [ ] remove advance_to_fn from range_fwd (is superseded by advance)
  - [ ] check license in new files
  - [ ] check for uses of `std::ref` instead of `ranges::ref`

Make most of range-v3 constexpr:
- [ ] core:
  - [x] `begin`/`end`/`rbegin`/`rend`...
  - [x] `at`/`size`/`empty`/`front`/`back`
  - [x] `move` + `indirect_move`
  - [x] `swap` (doesn't add std::swap to ADL anymore because it is not constexpr)
  - [ ] `distance`
    - rethink distance as customization point
  - [ ] note: add issue `data` non-member function 
  - [ ] `range_adaptor`: discuss with eric the mutable member:  `/*mutable*/ base_range_t rng_;` 
- [x] utility:
  - [x] `variant` impl is not constexpr and works (at least for the tests)
    - Note: feels like duck-tape, I think it is better to reconsider the design of `tagged_variant` from scratch. For example Eggs.Variant is a 1:1 constexpr-compliant replacement to `tagged_variant`, with:
      
      ``` c++
         template<typename... Ts>
         using tagged_variant = eggs::variant<Ts...>;
         using eggs::variants::get;
         template<std::size_t I, typename...Ts, typename U>
         RANGES_RELAXED_CONSTEXPR
      ```

title: constexpr algorithms
body:
add constexpr support to the following core facilities:
- distance / enumerate
- range / sized_range / make_range / range::get
- range_iterface
  add constexpr support to the following facilities in utility/functional:
- as function
- with_braced_init_args
- operators
- reference_wrapper
- ref_fn / ref
- add greater as a synonym for operator> (requires WeaklyOrdered and EqualityComparable)
  add c++14 constexpr support to utility/move
  add c++14 constexpr support to safe_int and add constexpr swap function to safe_int
  bugfix: set_difference test

The following algorithms can be used within constexpr functions with minimal to no changes to the 
algorithm implementation: 
- adjacent_find
- all_of
- any_of
- binary_search
- copy
- copy_backward
- copy_if
- copy_n
- count
- count_if
- equal
- equal_range
- fill
- fill_n
- find
- find_end
- find_first_of
- find_if
- find_if_not
- for_each
- generate
- generate_n
- includes
- inplace_merge (unbuffered)
- is_heap
- is_heap_until
- is_partitioned
- is_sorted
- is_sorted_until
- lexicographical_compare
- lower_bound
- make_heap
- max_element
- merge
- merge_move
- min_element
- minmax_element
- mismatch
- move
- move_backward
- none_of
- partition
- partition_copy
- partition_move
- partition_point
- push_heap
- random_shuffle (for user-provided constexpr random number generators)
- remove
- remove_copy
- remove_copy_if
- remove_if
- replace
- replace_copy
- replace_copy_if
- replace_if
- reverse_copy
- rotate
- rotate_copy
- search
- search_n
- set_difference
- set_intersection
- set_symmetric_difference
- set_union
- shuffle\* (for user-provided constexpr uniform random number generators)
- sort_heap
- stable_partition
- stable_sort
- swap_ranges
- transform
- unique
- unique_copy
- upper_bound

[*] shuffle: requires a constexpr uniform_int_distribution that has been adapted from 
libc++ (with minimal changes), but no real changes to the algorithm itself. For testing purposes, the linear_congruential_engine from libc++ has been adapted (with minimal changes).

The following algorithms haven’t been adapted yet because goto is not allowed within constexpr functions and as a consequence the algorithms would have to be rewritten: 
- nth_element
- is_permutation

This is doable, and I partially did so for stable_partition, but I would like to know what you think.

The following algorithms are constexpr but use iter_swap. Since iter_swap requires indirect_swap and thus swap to be constexpr, they won’t be constexpr for most types (e.g. int, they work for `safe_int<int>` because it has a constexpr swap): 
- sort_heap
- pop_heap
- inplace_merge
- next_permutation
- partial_sort
- partial_sort_copy
- partition
- prev_permutation
- random_shuffle
- reverse
- shuffle
- stable_partition
- swap_ranges

I’ve tested these with safe_int by adding a friend swap function to safe_int. It might be better to add this functions for testing only, and not in general to safe int, since it overrides the default swap for the underlying type and does not perform ADL. 

On the usage of temporary buffers (note this discussion is now taking place in [this issue](https://github.com/ericniebler/range-v3/issues/168)):

I think it is :
- wrong for algorithms to allocate memory by default,
- even wronger that users cannot opt out of this behavior,
- bad that users cannot pass these algorithms preallocated buffers.

In libstdc++ and libc++ get_temporary_buffer just calls new in a loop. 
So even tho I can understand the good intentions behind get_temporary_buffer, I think that the way this is handled by the STL right now is far from optimal. 

The algorithms that use it directly are:
- stable_partition
- inplace_merge

And the algorithms that use these algorithms are:
- stable_sort

I’ve provided these algorithms with a constexpr member function called `inplace` that uses no buffer.
It will be better to provide them with another member function called `with_buffer` that allows the user to specify a buffer (such a stack allocated buffer). 

I'd rather leave this as is (with inplace) and open an issue where we can discuss this on its own, since I think is one of the things that is worth to get right on an STL2 (and maybe try to unify get_temporary_buffer with Allocator).

title: Update Concepts for decomposition design

As discussed in ericniebler/stl2#10.

Note that `ConstructibleRef` is a positively terrible name for "Constructible object or reference type."

Also, I'm not convinced that `CopyConstructible<Foo> && Movable<Foo>` is a meaningful constraint for algorithms that want to memoize the return value of a projection a la adjacent_difference. body:
Some views mutate its state on begin/end (e.g. `view::remove_if` on begin).  
This patch constrains `view::group_by` and `view::split` `begin_cursor` on `Range<const Rng>()`
to disable the const overload for these kinds of ranges (such that the non-const overload
is picked up instead).

body:
`tagged_variant` constructors and `set` are now variadic. Note that the variadic implementation of `construct_fun` is an egregious hack with `const_cast` since the visitation implementation wants visitors to be immutable, but I want to perfect forward the constructor arguments.

Drive-by: reduce redundant code by using a common implementation for `tagged_variant` move/copy constructor/assignment, and another for detail::variant_data copy/move.
